title: Job 1:6–12
context: The narrator now turns to a heavenly scene. On the day when “God’s sons” come to present themselves before the LORD, Satan also comes among them. The LORD and Satan speak; Job is named “my servant,” blameless and upright; Satan challenges the worth of that fear of God and asks that the hedge around Job be removed. The LORD places all that Job has in Satan’s power, with a limit: “Only on himself don’t stretch out your hand.” The speakers are the narrator, the LORD, and Satan. WEB’s wording is “Satan” throughout; whether the term is here a title, the satan or the adversary, or a personal name is discussed, and the notes do not build a fuller biography than the scene itself gives. “God’s sons” are best read as heavenly beings who present themselves before the LORD; stronger identifications should be hedged. The difference between a permission and a decree in the LORD’s words at 1:12 is real and should be handled fairly in the regular notes, not by a new keyContrast. The existing box at Judges 9:23, and the census notes at 2 Samuel 24:1 and 1 Chronicles 21:1, already treat how God’s rule relates to evil agents. Shared ground must stay explicit: God is not the author of evil; Satan acts only within the limits God sets; and, as 1:22 and 2:10 will confirm, Job is not charged with sin. Classical Arminians, here as elsewhere, affirm exhaustive foreknowledge; the LORD’s questions in this scene are not to be read as open-theist ignorance. Both traditions take the unit as the heavenly origin of the coming losses, under a real bound.

verses.text: Now on the day when God’s sons came to present themselves before the LORD, Satan also came among them.
verses.arminianNotes:
The narrator says that “on the day when God’s sons came to present themselves before the LORD, Satan also came among them.” “God’s sons” are heavenly beings in this scene, appearing before the LORD; more exact identifications, such as a particular order of angels, may be offered but should be held loosely. WEB calls the other speaker “Satan.” Some readers take the word as a title, the adversary, rather than as a proper name; Zechariah 3:1–2 also shows Satan standing as an adversary in a heavenly scene, a related text not to be forced into one setting with this one. The notes follow WEB’s wording and do not build beyond what this verse says.

Arminian readers take the gathering as a real heavenly court, Satan present among God’s sons, not as a mere parable of inner struggle.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also read heavenly beings before the LORD, with Satan coming among them, a scene the narrator reports as taking place, not as a dream of Job’s.

Both traditions keep the identity of God’s sons and the name-or-title question hedged, and they invent no contrast over the terms.

verses.text: The LORD said to Satan, “Where have you come from?” Then Satan answered the LORD, and said, “From going back and forth on the earth, and from walking up and down in it.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD asks Satan, “Where have you come from?” Satan answers, “From going back and forth on the earth, and from walking up and down in it.” The question and the answer belong to the dialogue the narrator records. They do not require the conclusion that the LORD lacked knowledge of Satan’s movements. Classical Arminians affirm exhaustive foreknowledge and should not be read as open theists here; Reformed readers likewise deny that God is informed as if from ignorance.

Arminian readers take the exchange as the opening of a real trial of the question that will follow, God already knowing Job, and already knowing the adversary, while still putting the question in the court.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also refuse an ignorant God. The LORD speaks; Satan reports a going to and fro on the earth; the scene moves to Job, not because heaven has just learned of him.

Both traditions keep the dialogue as the book’s way of opening the case, without a contrast over divine knowledge.

verses.text: The LORD said to Satan, “Have you considered my servant, Job? For there is no one like him on the earth, a blameless and an upright man, one who fears God, and turns away from evil.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says, “Have you considered my servant, Job? For there is no one like him on the earth, a blameless and an upright man, one who fears God, and turns away from evil.” The wording matches the narrator’s portrait in 1:1, now spoken by the LORD, who calls Job “my servant”. The initiative in naming Job is the LORD’s, not Satan’s. The question “Have you considered” is a bringing of Job forward in the scene, not a confession that God has only now noticed him. Exhaustive foreknowledge remains affirmed in both traditions.

Arminian readers hear the LORD’s own commendation as the truth about Job, a genuine righteousness the coming test will not rewrite as a fiction.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also start from the LORD’s verdict: there is no one like Job on the earth. The servant is already known and already praised, the same blameless and upright man as in 1:1.

Both traditions take the LORD’s words as the book’s measure of Job, and they invent no contrast over the question’s form.

verses.text: Then Satan answered the LORD, and said, “Does Job fear God for nothing?
verses.arminianNotes:
Satan answers, “Does Job fear God for nothing?” The charge is that Job’s piety is interested, a fear of God that depends on what Job receives. The speaker is Satan, and the question is an accusation, not the book’s verdict. The next verse will spell out the hedge Satan has in mind.

Arminian readers take the question as a real slander against a genuine fear of God, a claim that must be tested without being granted in advance.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also leave the sentence in Satan’s mouth, an accusation against the servant the LORD has just praised, not a doctrine the narrator has endorsed.

Both traditions keep the charge distinct from the book’s own estimate of Job, and they invent no contrast over the motive Satan imputes.

verses.text: Haven’t you made a hedge around him, and around his house, and around all that he has, on every side? You have blessed the work of his hands, and his substance is increased in the land.
verses.arminianNotes:
Satan continues, “Haven’t you made a hedge around him, and around his house, and around all that he has, on every side? You have blessed the work of his hands, and his substance is increased in the land.” The hedge and the blessing are described as the LORD’s doing. Even the accuser ascribes Job’s safety and increase to God. The picture agrees with the prosperity of 1:2–3, now named as a divine hedge.

Arminian readers hear, even from Satan, that God has truly blessed Job and truly guarded him, a protection Satan wants removed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also take the hedge as the LORD’s, a real blessing around Job, his house, and all he has, which the coming permission will in part lift.

Both traditions receive the description of the hedge as accurate in substance, without taking Satan’s motive as their own.

verses.text: But stretch out your hand now, and touch all that he has, and he will renounce you to your face.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The challenge is, “But stretch out your hand now, and touch all that he has, and he will renounce you to your face.” Satan asks that the LORD’s hand be stretched out, and predicts that Job will renounce God openly. The predicted sin is the same verb Job feared in his children in 1:5. The speaker is still Satan; the prediction is his, not the narrator’s.

Arminian readers take the dare as a real attack on Job’s integrity, a claim that fear of God will fail if the gifts are touched.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also leave the forecast in Satan’s mouth. The hand to be stretched out is spoken of as the LORD’s, though 1:12 will place the power in Satan’s hand under a limit; the two ways of speaking will need to be held together, as in the notes on the next verse and in the existing discussion at Judges 9:23.

Both traditions refuse to treat the predicted renouncing as already true, and they invent no new box here.

verses.text: The LORD said to Satan, “Behold, all that he has is in your power. Only on himself don’t stretch out your hand.” So Satan went out from the presence of the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says, “Behold, all that he has is in your power. Only on himself don’t stretch out your hand.” Satan then goes out from the LORD’s presence. The limit is express: Job’s person is not to be touched; all that he has is placed in Satan’s power. Shared ground should be stated plainly. God is not the author of evil. Satan acts only within the bound God sets. Job will not be charged with sin for what now befalls him (see 1:22; 2:10). The remaining difference is how to name the LORD’s act: Arminian readers typically hear a permission, God allowing and strictly limiting the adversary’s action, with exhaustive foreknowledge of what will follow, without God being the author of the raiders’ violence or the coming deaths. Reformed readers typically hear a sovereign decree that governs even this agency, as at Judges 9:23 and in the census notes at 2 Samuel 24:1 and 1 Chronicles 21:1, while still denying that God is the author of sin. That question already has a box; it should not be restated as a new keyContrast here.

Arminian readers therefore take “in your power” as a real, bounded permission, Satan going out to do only what has been allowed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same words as God’s governing will, the adversary acting as a secondary agent under a real limit, “Only on himself don’t stretch out your hand.”

Both traditions agree on the limit, on God’s holiness, and on Job’s innocence of what is about to fall, and they point to Judges 9:23 and the census notes rather than opening a new contrast.
